Decision: 25 people take the eliminate-with-severance path, 0 take the retrain-and-keep-current-pay path, and 100 take the retrain-and-move-to-plant-pay path.

Reasoning: The 125 roles are no longer needed, so the $11.4 million annual saving is secured on every path. The choice is how to treat the people. Retraining at plant pay costs about $60,600 per person once ($15,000 instruction plus $45,600 pay and benefits during training). That cost is paid back within two years against hiring from outside, and the plants hire about 500 people a year into roles these employees can fill. So retraining creates real value rather than just a cost.

The keep-current-pay path adds a recurring $16,560 per person per year, about $2.1 million a year for all 125, for as long as they hold the plant role. It buys little beyond avoiding a pay cut, and that recurring cost erodes the saving. I therefore assign none to it.

Eliminating roles costs only about $8,902 per person in severance and is the cheapest immediate option, but it forgoes the retraining payback for people the Company is hiring for anyway. I keep a minority on this path, 25 people, to limit the one-time spend and to give those for whom a plant role is a poor fit, notably business and financial staff facing a 39.8% pay reduction, a clear exit with severance.

The one-time cost is roughly $6.1 million for retraining plus about $0.2 million severance, comfortably within the $44.1 million of cash above minimum operating level, so no borrowing is needed. The split is applied in the same proportion to both functions. The main risk is the pay reduction for business and financial staff, which should be managed through individual conversations and support during the move.

Decision: 115 of the 125 affected people are retrained and moved into plant roles at the plant role's pay; 10 are retrained and moved into plant roles keeping their current pay; none have their roles eliminated.

Reasoning: The 125 roles' work is gone whatever happens, so the $11.4 million saving is secured on every path. The paths differ in cost and in outcome for the people. Retraining into plant roles costs $15,000 each plus $45,600 in pay during the six months of training, roughly $60,600 once per person, and that cost pays back within two years compared with external hiring. That makes the plant-pay path the best value: it keeps people employed and fills real hiring needs at no recurring cost beyond what the plant role already pays.

I have made the plant-pay path the main route. Its drawback is the pay reduction, which is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%) but severe for business and financial operations staff (39.8%). I have therefore placed 10 people on the keep-current-pay path, roughly $166,000 a year, to protect the employees facing the steepest cuts. Cash above the minimum operating level ($44.1 million) covers the one-time costs of all paths comfortably.

Risks: the 39.8% pay cut could cause attrition among business and financial staff even on the plant-pay path, and the retraining timeline (six months) must be managed. I recommend monitoring retention in the first year and revisiting the mix of keep-pay placements if attrition rises.

I have decided to retrain and move all 125 affected people, 70 from office and administrative support and 55 from business and financial operations, into plant roles at the plant role's pay. None will be eliminated and none will keep their current pay.

The work of these 125 roles is no longer needed, so the $11.4 million annual cost is saved on every path. The choice is therefore about what each path costs once and what it costs ongoing. Retraining all 125 costs $1.9 million in instruction and materials plus $5.7 million in pay and benefits during six months of training, about $7.6 million in total, a one-time cost. It is funded from cash above the minimum operating level of $44.1 million, which this covers without new borrowing.

The plant-pay path is the best of the three because it avoids the ongoing cost of the keep-pay path, which adds $16,560 per person per year, or $2.1 million a year for all 125. Our plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles. Moving these employees fills roles we would otherwise fill by hiring, and the retraining pays back in two years against outside hiring. Severance for all 125 would cost only about $1.1 million, but it would end the employment of people we could redeploy into roles we are already hiring for, and it would forgo that hiring saving.

I decided on 95 people moved to plant roles at plant pay, 20 moved to plant roles keeping current pay, and 10 eliminated with severance, across the 125 affected roles in office and administrative support and business and financial operations.

The main reason is cost and value. Moving people into plant roles fills positions the plants would otherwise hire for from outside, which the board pack says happens about 500 times a year. Each such move pays back its $15,000 retraining cost in two years, and the training wages ($45,600 per person) are paid either way because the person stays on payroll. Severance is the cheapest path in the first year, at about $8,902 each, but it gives up the plant-role value and sends people out of the Company.

I limited the keep-pay path to 20 people. It costs about $16,560 per person per year in recurring pay difference, which for 20 people is roughly $331,000 a year. That is a permanent cost, so I used it only to soften the hardest case. The plant-pay cut is the real concern: a business and financial operations employee would lose 39.8% of pay. Some of those people will likely need the keep-pay option, and I would rather offer it than force them out. Office and administrative staff take only a 1.5% cut, so most of them can move at plant pay without serious hardship.

I kept a small severance group, 10 people, for those who choose to leave. Their cost is one-time and modest, and it respects their choice. Total one-time cost is well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The split applies in proportion across both functions, and I would review the numbers after I see how many people accept each option.
